spec.name: Dutch Windmill
spec.description: A chunky, pastel Animal Crossing-style Dutch windmill: a tapering octagonal cream tower on a brick plinth, a teal shingled cap, four big cloth-and-lattice sails, a tail pole with winch, and a cosy porch door with flower boxes and flour sacks.
spec.layout:
Front is +Z, up is +Y, the model is centred on x=0 and stands on y=0. It is a toy-like windmill with soft rounded shapes, thick cream trim, oversized windows and warm pastel flat colours.

OCTAGONAL TOWER (apothem = centre to flat face): the plinth is y 0..0.5 with apothem 2.5 (circumradius 2.71) in brick, with a stone course on top. The tower rises from y 0.5 to y 5.0 and tapers linearly from apothem 2.2 at y 0.5 to apothem 1.45 at y 5.0 (circumradius 2.38 to 1.57). Every octagon has flat faces at the cardinal directions and vertices at 22.5 degrees, so a flat face points at +Z. The plinth, tower, curb and cap ring all use this orientation. Face azimuths run from +Z toward +X (the model's left): 0 = front, 45 = front-left, 90 = left, 135, 180 = back, 225, 270 = right, 315 = front-right. The tower body is cream plaster with soft horizontal shade bands, brick-red corner quoins and two thin brick bands at y 2.2 and y 4.3.

DOOR AND PORCH: the front-left face (azimuth 45, outward dir [0.707,0,0.707]) holds the door at doorCenter [1.56,0.5,1.56]. A small covered porch projects to apothem 3.1 (box x/z 0.8..3.0) with a roof at y 2.5. It stays clear of the front sail, which only occupies |x|<0.6 below the hub.

CAP: it rotates on the cap joint, sits on the curb at y 5.0, and is a rounded boat/dome shape with teal shingle rows. The ridge runs front to back. Cap radius is about 1.75 at the eaves (y 5.15) and the top is about y 6.95. A snout housing at the front reaches z 2.0 and holds the sail shaft. There is a finial and a small round window, and a weather vane sits on top.

SAILS: the rotor joint is at the hub [0,5.9,2.1] with its axis along +Z. The shaft nose and hub boss run z 2.1..2.75. The sails lie in the plane z=2.45 in a rest '+' shape (arms up, down, left, right), each 4.6 m from the hub centre to its tip. Each sail has a thick wooden stock, a lattice frame about 1.1 wide from r=1.0 to r=4.6, cream cloth panels on the trailing half, and a red stripe and tip cap. The sail tip reaches y 10.5 at the top and y 1.3 at the bottom, with x +-4.6.

TAIL: a tail pole runs from the cap's back (mount capBack [0,5.5,-1.7]) sloping down to a ground stake at [0,0,-4.3]. It carries a spoked winch wheel, a ladder, and a small bunting streamer.

STYLE: everything is a simple chunky base shape, slightly oversized and softened, with small details as separate parts in their own flat colours: cream trim rings, rounded window frames, shingle rows, rivets, flower dots. No part is textured or realistic. Warm tones sit on top and cooler tones underneath. Make a window glass pane glow soft yellow with the glow kit. Only small cosy props are included (flower boxes, sacks, barrel, lantern). No ground plane.

parts.builds: The brick plinth (y 0..0.5, apothem 2.5) with a stone cap course, brick base bands, and the tapering octagonal cream plaster tower (apothem 2.2 down to 1.45, y 0.5..5.0) as faceted lathes, extrudes or lofts. It has plaster shade bands, brickDark corner quoins up all 8 vertical edges, brick bands at y 2.2 and 4.3, and a cream trim ring and brick curb at y 5.0 (apothem 1.55..1.62, top at y 5.15). Windows go on faces 90, 270, 135, 225 and 315 only; the door face 45 and the front face 0 are left plain except for a plaster patch. Each window has a chunky cream frame, sill and lintel, a glassBlue pane (glow the pane with the glow kit) and wood shutters with small heart or diamond cut-outs. There is a round window at face 315. The back face 180 gets a loft hatch with a hoisting beam, a small pulley and a rope with a hook. Add a few stone patches and brick patches on the plinth, and a little lantern on a bracket at face 270. Cosy rounded Animal Crossing look; no door on this part.
parts.attaches: Rests on the floor at ground. Its top meets the cap at mount towerTop / capCurb. The door, porch and flower boxes on face 45 belong to porchDoor, which attaches at doorCenter and porchFloor.

parts.builds: The rotating cap on the cap joint, sitting on capCurb. It has a flush cream ring on the curb and a rounded boat-shaped dome in roofTeal. Its eaves radius is about 1.75 at y 5.15 and the top is about y 6.95, with an elongated snout reaching z 2.0 at capFrontShaft and a shorter tail end at z -1.9. It has rows of shingles (small overlapping plates alternating roofTeal, roofTealLight and roofTealDark), a cream ridge beam with a gold finial ball, and a weather vane (metal arrow and gold ball) on top. The front snout has a wood face-plate with the shaft bearing hole (the shaft nose is built by sails), and a small round porthole window with a cream frame on each side. A pair of short wood brackets sits at capBack to take the tail pole. Add a bargeboard trim in trimCream along the front gable edge, and a few leaf-shaped clay accents.
parts.attaches: Sits on the tower curb (mounts towerTop, capCurb). Its front snout meets the sails shaft at capFrontShaft / hub. Its back meets the tail pole at capBack.

parts.builds: The whole rotor on the rotor joint: a wood shaft from inside the cap nose out to z 2.75, a rounded wood hub boss with a gold nose cap and rivet ring at hub / sailPlane, and four identical sails in a '+' shape (up, down, left, right) in the plane z=2.45, each 4.6 m from the hub centre to its tip. Each sail has a thick wooden stock (woodLight) along its axis, and a lattice frame about 1.1 wide from r=1.0 to r=4.6 with two woodDark side rails and cross bars every 0.4 m. Cream sailCloth panels fill the trailing half of the frame (a few panels in each lattice cell, slightly rolled at the edge) with a sailRed stripe and a red tip cap. Small gold bolts sit at the bar crossings, and each tip has a small wood finial. A little cream pennant on the top sail tip. Build each sail once with a helper and rotate it for the other three.
parts.attaches: Shaft enters the cap snout at capFrontShaft; hub at mount hub. Keep the lowest sail tip above y 1.1. It must clear the porch roof (x >= 0.8 at the porch).

parts.builds: The tail pole and its fittings, riding the cap joint. A thick woodLight beam runs from the cap back at capBack [0,5.5,-1.7] sloping down to tailStake [0,0,-4.3] with a rounded end. Two A-frame braces sit near the cap, with a wood ladder (two rails and rungs) alongside the pole's lower half. A chunky spoked winch wheel (woodDark rim, wood spokes, gold hub, metal axle) is mounted on two posts at about 1/3 up the pole. A fat rope (cream, a few coil segments) is wound on the winch. A wood ground stake at tailStake carries a metal ring and ground rope loops and has a small stone footing, plus a red-and-cream bunting streamer of 5 small flags hanging between the pole and the cap. Small leafy sprigs at the stake base in leaf green.
parts.attaches: Top ends at capBack on the cap joint. The foot stake rests on the floor at tailStake.

parts.builds: Everything on tower face 45 (outward dir [0.707,0,0.707]) plus the cosy props. The door on joint doorHinge is a rounded-arch wood door in doorBlue with woodDark plank lines, a gold knob, strap hinges and a small round window. It has a thick cream frame with an arch, a keystone and a nameplate. The porch is a small covered stoop projecting to apothem 3.1 (centre porchFloor [2.19,0.5,2.19]) with a stone slab floor, two chunky wood posts with brackets, a lean-to roof of roofTeal shingle rows at y 2.5 (porchRoof) with a cream fascia, and two stone steps down to the ground. Above the door sits a round glowing glowYellow window with a cream frame. Props: two window flower boxes (wood, pink and yellow flowers, leaf green) on the porch rails, two sacks of flour (sack, tied necks, small ink-coloured label marks) and one wood barrel with metal hoops beside the steps, a hanging lantern (metal frame, glowYellow glass, glowing) under the porch roof, and a small welcome mat. Keep every prop chunky and rounded.
parts.attaches: Backs on tower face 45 at doorCenter and plinthTop, with the door hinging at doorHinge. The porch floor starts at y 0.5 on the plinth, steps reach y 0. The porch roof stays below the sail plane region (sails only occupy |x|<0.6 below y 5).

calls.reasoning:
I'm sketching the structure for a Dutch windmill in Animal Crossing style, planning a joint hierarchy with a root base, a cap, and a rotating hub for the sails so they can spin.

Now I'm working through realistic yet stylized proportions: an octagonal tapering tower around 5-6m tall, a boat-shaped cap roughly 1.2m high, and sails spanning about 9m across mounted on a hub near the top, making sure the lowest sail tip clears the ground via a small gallery stage. I'm calculating overall bounding dimensions—height near 10.7m and width near 9.4m—accounting for the sail arms' reach beyond the tower itself.

I'm settling on a soft Animal Crossing-inspired palette: cream plaster walls, a red-orange brick plinth, and warm terracotta tones for the cap, keeping everything rounded and pastel rather than harshly realistic.

Now I'm working out the windmill's sail geometry — positioning the hub and shaft forward from the tapered cap, figuring out the sail plane's offset so it clears the tower radius at ground level, and sizing the sail arms to extend well above and below the hub for a balanced silhouette.

I realize the gallery platform would collide with the lowest sail tip, so I'm skipping the stage structure and reconsidering door placement — since the sails sweep in front at z 2.35, I need to offset the door off-center rather than dead-center on the front face to avoid it being blocked by the rotating arm.

I'll place the door on the face at 45° toward +X with a small porch step and window above, plus a side balcony, and add a simple stone ring base with a round step. Now I'm breaking the mill into five parts, starting with the tower base — tapered octagon walls, brick bands, corner trim, plaster, door, windows, steps, dentils, and lanterns, sized as a box roughly 5.4 units wide and 5 tall with a budget of 190 — followed by the cap with a ring curb and a rounded terracotta dome.

Now I'm detailing the remaining pieces: the sails rotor with a hub boss, shaft, four lattice-framed sails with cloth and spars, and the tail and gallery assembly, including the fantail wheel and tail pole with winch and ladder descending to ground level.

I'll add a round stone path pad and a small signboard near the entrance, keeping props modest for that Animal Crossing charm. The door, porch, steps, shutters, flower boxes, sacks, and barrel belong to part 5 "doorway," positioned where the door face meets the tower, while sail blades extend horizontally near the top separate from this cluster.

Actually, I realize placing the door on a cardinal face near the sails risks collision, so instead I'll put the door on a 45° diagonal face of the octagonal tower, away from the rotating sail plane. I'm working out the apothem radius at ground level tapering upward to position the door opening correctly on that angled face.

Now I'm working out the tower's geometry in detail: the door mount position and orientation, the plinth's apothem and circumradius from 0 to 0.5, the tapering tower body from 0.5 to 5.0, and the cap curb, overhang ring, and dome proportions up to the top at 7.0, including where the hub element should sit near the cap front.

I'm also figuring out the rotor joint placement, sail arm lengths and their extent above and below hub height, overall bounding box dimensions accounting for the symmetric sails and front porch, and the tail pole's position and length running from the cap back down and outward.

For the floor and joint rig, I'm marking the tail pole's foot as the floor-touching point while leaving the sails and rotor exempt. Then I'm setting up the joint hierarchy: mill as root spine, cap as hinge child of mill, and rotor as a hinge child of cap grouped with the sails—plus considering a door hinge joint off mill for the door builder to use.

Now I'm working out the door hinge's exact position, placing it along the tangent of the tower face at 45 degrees offset from the door center, and reconciling how the door sits flush against the plinth top where the plinth's wider apothem meets the tower face.

I'm then positioning the porch so it extends outward from the plinth at a larger apothem, checking its corner coordinates against the tower's footprint to confirm the width and placement stay within reasonable bounds on both sides.

Now I'm settling on a color palette capped at 24 swatches, picking out cream and shaded plaster tones, brick reds, stone grays, and switching the roof to a teal-green shingle look with a lighter accent, plus trim whites and wood tones for structural details.

Rounding out the palette with sail cloth and frame colors, striped red sail accents, glowing window glass, ink outlines, floral pinks and yellows, leaf green, metal gray, and gold accents—landing right around 24 total. Then I'm breaking the model into five main parts: the tower body with its bands and multi-level windows, the cap, the rotor, the tail and fan assembly, and the porch.

Checking the triangle budget across parts—180, 170, 230, 120, 160—comes to 860, safely under the 900 cap, with the door attached to the porch via a hinge joint. I'm also noting the overall style: rounded and chunky with soft pastels, thick trim, oversized windows, flat colors, and small leaf/flower motifs suggesting stitched cloth. Now I need to write precise layout instructions so builders stay aligned—specifying the tower's apothem formula, confirming the octagon orientation with flat faces toward cardinal directions and vertices at 22.5°, and detailing the cap geometry including curb height and dome profile radius.

I'm working out the cap's full shape rising to a top height of 6.9, extended forward into a snout for the shaft housing, with a front gable and ridge along the z-axis, plus mount points for the hub, tower top, cap back, door center, and front shaft. For the sails, I'm detailing each arm's wooden spar length and radius, the lattice frame with rails and cross bars, and cream cloth panels with red stripe pennants at the tips, along with precise width and radius dimensions for the sail frame.

Now I'm placing the sail plane position and hub boss, then moving to the tail assembly: a tail pole running from the cap back down to a ground stake, with a spoked winch wheel, ladder rungs, cross braces, a stake post with ring, a sagging rope, and maybe a small lantern and flag at the end, all within a budgeted part count for the tail section.

I'm then working out which bounding box each part occupies so the tower, porch, and tail pieces don't overlap incorrectly, deciding that the porch owns the door, frame, surround, and window above the door, while the tower owns side windows placed away from the front sail shaft so they aren't obstructed by it.

I'm naming faces by azimuth angle and assigning windows at the left/right (90/270), front-right (315), and diagonal (135/225) positions at varying heights, plus a back hatch door at the top with a hoisting beam for loft access. Now I'm ready to write the final JSON with descriptions that are thorough but concise.

I'm planning the buildSails function, placing the rotor joint at the hub with a +Z axis and positioning the sail geometry using the rotor bone, with the sail plane set at z=2.45.

I'm working out a helper to place each sail at an angle around the hub: computing direction and perpendicular vectors from theta, then figuring the right rotation offset so the box's local Y axis aligns with the arm direction, and deriving a position function combining the hub location with radial and lateral offsets plus vertical height above the sail plane.

Now I'm sizing the sail components for each arm, starting with the main stock box—its width, thickness, and length spanning from near the hub out to the tip, checking that the extreme positions stay within reasonable bounds relative to the hub height.

Then I'm adding side rails flanking the stock, end bars at both extremes, and cross bars spaced evenly along the frame to give the sail its lattice structure.

Bolts would balloon the part count if placed individually at every crossing, so I'll merge them into one geometry per sail to stay within budget—roughly 55 parts allotted per sail across stock, rails, bars, cloth, bolts, and trim.

Since bolts are spheres and rotationally symmetric, I can just compute their positions directly in model space and translate, skipping rotation matrices entirely. Now I need to figure out which side of the stock counts as the trailing half for cloth placement, using the local x-axis orientation relative to the arm angle.

For the cloth panels, I'm placing nine small box panels in the lattice cells, sized to fit within each cell's gap and positioned just behind the bars. I'm also considering adding a small cylinder along each panel's lower edge to suggest a slightly rolled fabric edge.

I'll switch to quaternion-based rotation for tilting the cloth, combining a yaw and tilt quaternion for the sail twist. For the red accents, I'm planning a longitudinal stripe near v=0.3 with a narrow width, plus a separate red tip cap.

Adding the tip cap and lattice cross bars...

Still working out panel placement...

Tallying parts: with 16 louvre panels per sail and the other components, I land around 140 for the sails, plus hub and pennant pieces, keeping the total safely under 230 with simple box geometry. I'm also considering adding a thin lengthwise lattice rod on the leading half of each arm for extra detail.

Now I'm working out cloth panel placement on the trailing half of each sail—centering subpanels with a gap between them, applying consistent tilt for a corrugated look, and setting up the hub shaft as a cylinder running along the central axis.

For the hub itself, I'm sketching it as a layered construction: a back flange cylinder in dark wood, then a main drum section in regular wood, building out the boss shape from stacked cylindrical segments rather than a single complex form.

I'm placing the rivets on the flange rim instead, since the drum covers the inner radius—putting eight small gold spheres at radius 0.46, z 2.28 around the visible flange band. Then I need to check the stocks crossing through the hub at the sail plane, since that depth range overlaps the drum's z-span.

Since both stock bars share the same depth and only overlap inside the drum, that's fine to leave coplanar. I'm also adding a metal band ring around the drum at r 0.44, z 2.4 with slight thickness, letting the stocks pass through it since they're on different surfaces and won't z-fight.

I'm adding gold bolts near the hub base of each stock, plus a dark wood "claw" block covering the stock root where the lattice begins. For the shaft, I'll add a metal collar ring near the cap's face plate around z 2.0-2.1 to suggest a bearing, accepting it might slightly overlap the cap plate.

For the top sail's tip, I'm designing a small pennant flag: a cone-shaped finial at the very top, with a thin mast rising from it and a triangular cream-colored flag extruded sideways to flutter off the mast.

I'll offset the pennant flag to extend from the mast toward -x, giving it a swallowtail shape with a small red stripe accent, and add a slight wave to its outline for a fluttering effect.

For the arm tips, I'm placing small cone-shaped wood finials pointing outward, sized and rotated so their axis aligns with the arm direction, checking that the lowest tip still clears the required height.

Now I'm setting up helper functions to build sail parts using position and rotation data, computing local coordinates for each sail based on angle, direction vectors, and offsets to place points correctly in 3D space.

I'm also planning the color palette, giving wood, sail cloth, gold, and trim distinct tones, and considering alternating sailCloth and plaster shades across panels for visual texture.

For the sail arms, I'm setting angles at 90, 270, 0, and 180 degrees for the plus shape, and adding a rolled trim cylinder along each arm positioned near the edge of the panel with a slight vertical lift, using the trimCream color for the rail detail.

Placing a red stripe to bridge the narrow gap between subpanels, then adding gold bolt spheres along the bars at front-facing positions calculated from the stock depth.

I'm merging 27 bolt spheres into a single geometry for efficiency, attaching it to the rotor bone, and adding a thin dark-wood rod along the leading edge for lattice slats, skipping diagonal bracing for now before moving on to writing the hub position code.

Now I'm constructing the hub itself from cylinders oriented along the Z axis: a central shaft spanning the hub's length, a ring of small rivet spheres embedded at the flange's front face, and the flange cylinder sized to fit around them.

Positioning the claw at radius 0.75 with length 0.5 so it sits between drum and lattice without overlap, and adding two bolts into it at radii 0.65 and 0.85. Then I'm setting up the pennant extrusion with its outline, thickness, and bone attachment, plus starting the mast as a thin box.

Adding the red stripe detail to the flag geometry, then finalizing the finial and pennant positioning before writing the actual mesh-building code with the necessary imports.

I'll keep the Ctx type as given in the function signature without importing it, since types erase at runtime anyway. For the tail pole geometry, I'm planning it to run from the back cap position down to a lower point behind.

Now I'm working out the exact coordinates — aiming the pole's rounded bottom end to sit near ground level, around y 0.2-0.3, with a slight radius so it doesn't clip below the floor, and considering adding a separate stake post near the pole's base to anchor it.

I'll use the rod helper for straight members with faceted low-poly sides (8 sides, smooth off) and set up the pole as a capsule between its two endpoints.

Working out the pole's geometry now: computing its start point, direction vector, and perpendicular normals so I can orient the top surface correctly since the pole slopes down and back.

I'll place the ladder lashed alongside the pole offset toward the back face, with rails parallel to the pole axis and rungs running crosswise, spanning the lower-to-mid section. Then I still need to position the winch posts roughly a third of the way up the pole.

I realize the wheel would collide with the pole at that radius, so I'm repositioning it to the side instead, with the axle running between two posts mounted on a cross-beam bracket at t=0.58, keeping everything offset from the pole's centerline.

Working out the wheel placement in the YZ-plane with the pole position at t=0.58, computing the center coordinates and radius bounds, then figuring out the support posts connecting the pole bracket points to the axle center.

Now I'm designing the wheel rim as a torus oriented along the x-axis with spokes radiating out to it from the center.

Next I'm adding a gold hub cylinder at the center, handle pegs sticking out at the spoke tips like capstan handles, and a wooden rope drum mounted on the axle to hold the coiled cream rope.

Checking clearance so the rope path from the drum to the stake ring stays just outside the pole radius along its length, interpolating z-position at each y value to confirm it doesn't clip the pole's surface.

I'm checking the ring's placement on the stake and noticing the stake and pole positions nearly overlap at the bottom — I need to nudge the stake further out to avoid the collision.

Skipping full rope lashing for simplicity, I'll add a small ring loop on the stake's side, positioning its torus so it just touches the stake's edge, plus a small eye bolt detail nearby.

For the rope, I'm adding flat coiled loops lying on the ground near the stake with a connecting curve from the ring down to them, then a stone footing cylinder at the pole's base and a few small rock shapes scattered around it.

I'm picking out the overall color palette for stone, wood, metal, sail cloth, and foliage tones, plus adding a couple A-frame braces near the top of the pole angling out to support the cap structure.

I'm working out where each A-frame brace's feet should attach along the cap's curved rim, checking whether the foot coordinates land inside or outside the dome radius at that height.

Adding iron collar details at the apexes, gold bolts at the feet, and banded rings around the pole with slight taper. I'm also throwing in a pivot block and planning small bunting flags strung between the pole and cap.

Placing flags along a sagging quadratic bezier curve between the cap and pole, alternating red and cream colors across five triangular flags, with a thin rope swept along the same curve connecting them.

I'm recalculating the string endpoints and sag between the cap and pole to avoid clashing with the A-frame legs, trying a few alternate anchor points on the right side so the bunting and flags sit clear of the structure.

I'm worried the leg line and bunting string might cross visually, so I'm adjusting the A-frame positions slightly and repositioning the bunting to run from lower on the pole out to the cap point, accepting a small overlap as fine.

Checking the bunting length and sag, I'll keep five flags hanging vertically, evenly spaced along the swag. But I realize the hook position at x=1.3 pokes outside the box bounds, so I need to pull it inward to around x=0.75-0.78, placing it right at the cap eave where the curb radius keeps it visible rather than buried inside the shell.

Now I'm adding leafy sprigs around the stake base using small angled cones for leaves plus sphere clumps for fullness, with five sprigs arranged around the base point using randomized variation for a natural look. For the ladder, I'm positioning the rails offset from the pole axis by the pole radius plus a small gap, running them along the top normal direction.

Widening the ladder to x ±0.27 with rail and rung radii set, spacing rungs roughly every 0.28 units along the pole, and checking the rail endpoints clear the floor properly.

Adjusting the pole offset to 0.16 so the ladder rails sit flush against the tapered pole surface without gaps, and verifying the rungs don't collide with the pole's inner radius at that distance. Now I'm setting up a small rod helper function to draw cylindrical connectors between points for the ladder structure.

Checking the capsule's round end cap doesn't poke through the pole's top bounds, then working out the vector math for the pole's direction and a perpendicular vector in the YZ plane to orient things correctly.

Writing box placement logic...

I'll simplify to just a few metal and dark wood bands near the stake ends instead of fussing over stripes. For the stake itself, I'm giving it a rounded top, sinking the base flush with the ground, and adding small cream rope loops as tori wrapped around it at a few heights, plus flat loops lying near the base on the ground.

I'm checking placement carefully so the ground loops don't clip into the stone footing -- shifting their position and radius so they clear the footing's extent, then planning a connecting rope curve running from the ring to the loop.

Now I need two rope segments: one from the drum wrapping to the stake's loops near the top, and another from the ring down to the ground loops. I'm figuring out the start point for the drum rope, offset from the drum's center.

Checking the rope curve clears the pole at multiple heights and ends properly looped around the stake, staying within radius constraints. Verifying overall structure heights stay within bounds, then moving to define the wheel rim torus geometry with its center, axis, and radius.

Adding wheel details, spokes, hub...

Positioning posts clear of the wheel radius, then adding rim pegs as small cylinders and checking the drum/rope placement doesn't clip the posts.

Still refining the drum and torus placement, aligning the rope start with the drum coils. I'm sketching helper functions for generating rods and part geometry, including options for thinner sides on small components.

Placing sprigs...

Checking footing placement...

Now I'm positioning sprigs around the stake, worried the ring radius pushes slightly outside the box at z=-4.5, so I'll tighten the radius and limit sprigs to angles facing front/sides rather than all around to avoid overflow.

I'm attaching the ring to the stake with a short connecting rod, adding a small metal collar torus on the stake, then working out the bunting string geometry—defining a bezier path from a hook point near the cap eave to a control point to a point on the pole, with a small metal ball marking the hook attachment.

Now I'm placing metal bands with loops along the pole at several positions, using one to anchor the string via a tiny gold bead, then moving to flag construction—extruding a triangular pennant outline along the path with proper orientation vectors, and considering adding a small contrasting trim stripe to the flags.

Adding flag trim triangles...

Revised total lands near 105, within budget. Now I'm working out the A-frame geometry: apex position offset from the pole, legs angling down to foot points, a crossbar connecting the legs partway down, and a metal collar torus wrapped around the pole at the apex height.

Setting the specific foot and apex coordinates for both A-frames to vary their height and spread slightly, then moving to the ladder setup... Placing the rails and rungs along the pole...

Now I'm defining helper functions for positioning points relative to the pole axis, then building out the winch structure: brackets, an axle, support posts, and diagonal braces, all with specific coordinates and wood materials for a sturdier mechanical look.

For the wheel itself, I'm working in the global YZ plane to place eight spokes radiating from the hub center at even angular intervals, adding a hub cylinder along the X-axis and pegs at each rim point.

Then I'm adding two rim tori offset slightly along X to give the wheel some thickness, checking that the spoke length and wheel radius keep everything positioned correctly relative to the ground. I'm verifying clearances — making sure the wheel doesn't clip the ladder or the rope hanging from the drum, checking the top and bottom y-extents against the pole and rope positions.

Now I'm defining the rope as a bezier curve running from the drum down to near the ground, choosing a cream/bone color to match the sack material, and setting up a sweep along that path with a small radius to give the rope its coiled form.

Then I'm adding the ground rope as a catmull-rom curve connecting the ring bottom to looped sections near the base, swept thin at radius .025, plus a couple of tori lying flat for the loops themselves, oriented so their axis points along world y. I'm also planning stake loops as tori wrapped around a vertical stake.

For the stake top I'm placing a small sphere cap, then building a footing with a cylinder base and scattering a few darker stone icosahedra around its perimeter at offset angles, flattened vertically and positioned to stay within the ground boundary.

Now I'm adding metal bands as torus rings around the pole at a few key heights, plus small gold bolt spheres on two of the bands, and finally placing a dark wooden pivot block at the top with gold bolts on its sides.

I'm setting up the flag positions along a quadratic bezier curve from the hook to the pole's end, alternating colors between sail red and cream with contrasting inner triangles so flags look good double-sided, while keeping a rough tally of the part budget to stay within limits.

Setting up imports for randomness and curve helpers...

I'm thinking through how to type the Ctx parameter for the towerBody function without conflicting with a possibly globally-provided Ctx type, deciding to avoid redeclaring it and instead use it inline safely.

For the geometry, I'm weighing a lathe-based octagon versus a rotated CylinderGeometry with 8 segments — rotating 22.5° about Y so a flat face faces each cardinal direction, keeping shading smooth above that segment threshold.

I'm planning a helper function that builds octagonal frusta from apothem values at bottom/top, driving the tower's tapering profile with a formula and layering slightly oversized thin frusta as plaster shade bands at specific height ranges for a soft horizontal shading effect.

Now I'm figuring out corner quoins as stacked alternating-width blocks placed at each of the eight vertical edges, tapering with the tower radius and rotated to face each corner's azimuth.

Realizing 8 corners × many blocks will blow through my part budget, so I decide to merge each quoin set into a single geometry using BufferGeometryUtils' mergeGeometries, keeping it as one part per color rather than dozens of individual boxes.

I'm setting up a color-keyed collector that accumulates box geometries with their transforms, then flushes each bucket into a merged part bound to the mill bone — keeping glow effects as separate parts since they need their own material.

For orienting elements onto the tower's faces, I'm working out that rotating around Y by the azimuth angle correctly aligns a local +Z axis with the outward direction, so each face-mounted piece (like windows) gets positioned and rotated based on that angle. I also need to account for the tower's taper — since the wall slopes inward by 1/6 per meter of height, I'm calculating a tilt angle of about 9.46° to keep windows and other face elements flush with the sloped surface.

Now I'm combining both rotations via quaternion composition (azimuth around Y, then tilt around X) to get the final orientation, and designing a placement helper that computes the position on the sloped face using the apothem function plus local offsets for lateral and outward placement.

Then I'm working out which faces get windows — placing round windows around y≈3.2-3.3 across faces 90, 270, 135, 225, and 315.

Checking face 315's round window position against the lower rectangular window, then settling on y 3.3 windows for faces 90/270 with shutters, and slightly different y 2.9 for 135/225, while placing the lantern on face 270 near y 2.0 below the sill.

I need to recheck the vertical spacing between the rectangular window, round window, and brick band on face 315 so they don't collide—adjusting the round window's radius and center height to keep clearance below the band.

Then I'm settling on a simpler scheme: keep most rectangular windows centered around y=3.0, with only minor variation across faces, and defining a reusable windowAt function that builds a frame box and glass pane positioned by azimuth and height.

For the glass panes, I'm adding thin mullion crosses for detail and deciding to make only some windows glow -- using glowYellow on the 270 and 135 faces for warmth while keeping glassBlue elsewhere for contrast.

I'm also adding a cream sill below each window and a lintel above, keeping the cap simple rather than adding extra decorative elements.

Positioning wood shutters flanking each window with subtle plank lines and a small heart-shaped cutout near the top for a cottage feel.

For the round window I'm building a lathed cream frame rotated so its axis runs along z, with a glowing yellow glass cylinder inset and cross mullions plus small gold rivets around the rim. Then I'm adding weathering details to the facade — a plaster patch and an exposed brick patch on certain faces to break up the uniform wall surface.

Face 45 is the door side, so I'll leave it plain since the porch belongs elsewhere. Now I'm working out the plinth geometry — a cylindrical octagon base with brick coloring, calculating apothem and circumradius values to make sure the base band extents fit within the bounding box without overshooting the vertex limits.

I need to avoid the porch floor conflicting with the stone course, so I'll keep the brick plinth from 0 to 0.42, then add a stone course from 0.42 to 0.5 with a slight overhang, flush with the tower base. I'll also add a small stepped stone chamfer just above that to transition cleanly into the tower.

Now I'm adding decorative detail: small stone and brick patches on the vertical plinth faces, plus horizontal brick row lines, using a helper placement function parametrized by apothem and tilt so I can reuse it for both flat plinth faces and angled surfaces later.

I'm also planning alternating quoin blocks at the 8 corners, spaced vertically from the base up to the top, slightly protruding to read as masonry edges while avoiding overlap with the door and lantern areas.

Working through the geometry, the wall radius at a given tangential offset follows R minus a factor times the offset, so I need to check how far the corner box protrudes relative to the wall edge at its sides versus its tip — the box ends up sticking out about 0.134 at the sides and 0.08 at the corner, which seems like it'll read as blocky quoins rather than a clean point.

I'm checking the step dimensions against the box corner constraint, adjusting the lower step width to 3.7 and u to ±0.8 so the diagonal corners stay within the 3.2 limit, verifying both front and side corner coordinates work out.

Now I notice there's a gap between the plinth edge and porch floor from w=2.5 to 3.1 that needs filling, so I'm adding a stone footing/skirt box there from ground level up to 0.5 height, using stone coloring to keep the stoop looking solid rather than hollow underneath.

Checking the boundary against the adjacent face, I confirm the point stays inside the octagon. I adjust the slab dimensions so corners stay within the box constraint while keeping edges aligned with the tower face plane.

I'm laying out the structural stack: plinth top at apothem 2.5, footing spanning w=2.4 to 3.1 with top overlapping the slab, and slab sitting from y=0.5 to 0.6. Steps use top heights of 0.2 and 0.4, and the porch floor sits at y=0.6, setting up where the door base should begin.

Now I'm working out the door geometry relative to that floor level—placing the threshold around y=0.6, defining the door outline with a straight section of height 0.85 topped by an arch of radius equal to the half-width, giving a total door height near 1.28 and a top edge around y≈1.78 or so once added to the base offset.

Factoring in the frame thickness and keystone pushes the overall opening height to roughly y≈2.0-2.08, which starts crowding the space where I wanted to put the nameplate and window above it—so I'm reducing the door half-width down to about 0.4 to free up vertical room.

With a straight door height of 0.75 and half-width 0.4, I'm recalculating the stacking: door top lands near y=1.74, the frame pushes it to about y=1.87, the keystone to roughly y=1.93, leaving room for a nameplate around y=2.02-2.12 and a window centered near y=2.4 with its frame spanning about y=2.22-2.58, before the roof underside meets the wall around y=2.62-2.72.

Now I'm second-guessing proportions — the door at 0.8 wide by 1.25 tall feels small against a tower with a 4.6 sail and 1.8m face width, but Animal Crossing-style scale with a ~1m character plus the porch roof constraint at 2.5 makes it work. I'm settling on a door half-width of 0.42, straight height 0.75, with a 0.15 frame band pushing the outer edge to 0.57 and jamb centers at u=±0.495.

Now working out the porch posts at u=±0.9, chunky 0.16x0.16 wood posts from y 0.6 to 2.3 with base and cap blocks, plus small triangular brackets connecting posts to a header beam. I'm calculating the roof underside height at w=3.0 using the slope formula, landing on a header beam top around 2.25 and bottom near 2.05.

Adding diagonal brace geometry and a hanging lantern with chain, metal frame, and glowing glass...

Checking whether the roof overhang clashes with the posts — side rails sit fine between wall and posts at w=3.0. But I need to verify the roof's back edge against the octagon's sloped walls near the corners, since the roof extends to u=±1.05 while the wall corner pulls inward at higher y — I should check if that roof point actually falls outside the octagon boundary.

Testing the roof's outer corner point against the adjacent face planes at u=±1.05, w=1.8: converting to the octagon's x/z coordinates, these points land outside the apothem distance for both adjacent faces, meaning the roof protrudes past the tower's side walls near the corners rather than intersecting them — so there's no collision, just an overhang.

But near u=0 the roof back edge sits slightly inside the wall (good contact), while near the ±0.77 corner where the wall plane retreats to the next face, a gap opens up and the roof edge appears to float away from the tower. I'm considering pulling the roof back edge inward to w=1.5 along a sloped taper so it keeps penetrating the adjacent faces and closes that visible gap.

Checking the slope math, extending the rise that far pushes the roof height slightly over the 2.75 box limit — I'm trying a shallower slope or starting the taper closer at w=1.55, accepting a tiny 0.02 overage as likely within tolerance.

Working out the rotation for the slab so it tilts correctly along the slope, applying a positive rotation about the X axis. Now I'm planning the shingle rows on top of the dark teal base slab, laying out roughly six rows across the slope.

I realize doing individual scalloped tabs per row would blow past my part budget, so instead I'll merge shingle geometry by color group—using mergeGeometries so each of the three teal shades becomes a single combined part rather than dozens of tiny boxes.

Tallying up part counts across all the components—door, frame, window, roof, posts, rails, flower boxes, sacks—to see how close I'm getting to the 160-part budget.

To cut this down, I'm planning a merge strategy where small repeated geometry gets batched by bone and color into shared meshes, since keeping every piece separate would blow past the limit. Glow effects need to stay as distinct parts since they wrap around other geometry rather than merging in, so I'll handle those through a direct path while everything else gets grouped, bringing the realistic part count down to something more like 20.

Flat shading works fine for the low-poly look across all merged geometry types since they share compatible indexed attributes, while extrude-based parts like the door slab and arch stay separate since they use their own bone transforms.

Writing transform and build logic...

Setting up a bucket system to group geometry by bone and color, with helper functions that place flat porch pieces and wall pieces using composed quaternions (base rotation times local euler rotation) for correct orientation.

I'm defining box and cylinder builder helpers that orient geometry along the right local axes using rotation arguments, then merging each bucket's geometries into a single mesh per bone at the end.

Now I'm settling on a color palette, sticking mostly to existing palette entries rather than inventing new hex colors.

For glow effects, I'm wrapping specific parts like the lantern glass and round window disc in solo glow calls with their own material, keeping the glow strength subtle.

I'm designing a helper function that places geometry with position, rotation, and scale, with an option to return it as a standalone glowing part when needed, applying non-uniform scaling directly to the geometry before positioning.

Now I'm working through the exact pieces of the model—starting with the footing and floor, using boxes sized and positioned to form a stone base with a darker trim band around it.

Adding slab overhang with a lip, then sketching flagstone joint lines across the top surface with dark seam marks.

For the porch itself, I'm placing a welcome mat near the doorway with a sail-red base, cream stripe accents, and a thin cream border box to frame it.

Then I'm working out the step geometry: an upper step and lower step with slightly different widths and heights so the lower step's tread extends out beyond the upper one, creating a proper staircase profile down to the porch floor.

Setting step bodies to stoneDark with thinner stone top plates stacked at the right heights for each step, and keeping the footing in stone for contrast against the darker steps.

Now I'm working out the posts: placing base blocks and vertical post boxes at ±0.9 offsets, sizing them to sit on the base and rise up to meet a header spanning between them.

Computing diagonal bracket struts connecting each post to center, working out the angle and rotation needed so the strut box aligns along the vector between post and center point.

Now I'm positioning the top and bottom side rails between the wall and front post, setting their dimensions and y-heights to match the porch railing proportions.

I'm adding three balusters evenly spaced along each rail, then adjusting the rail start point so it meets the tower corner cleanly without leaving a visible gap, recalculating the rail length and center accordingly.

For decoration, I'm placing a flower box on top of each rail, embedding it slightly into the rail surface, and adding a slightly larger rim piece in a lighter wood tone just above it for visual detail.

Now I'm populating the flower boxes with alternating pink and gold flower spheres with tiny cream centers, spaced across the box width with slight jitter, plus small green leaf clusters positioned around each flower for a fuller look.

Moving to the roof, I'm computing the sloped roof surface using the width-dependent height formula and the slope angle, then building a base slab sized and rotated to match that pitch, positioned within the porch's local coordinates.

Now I'm working out the shingle row layout along the roof slope, planning tab dimensions and spacing so each row overlaps the one below it like real shingles, with lower rows sitting on top of higher ones toward the front edge.

Working out tab row spacing and counts, settling on 6 rows at 0.28 spacing, and figuring out how to offset tabs across alternating rows so a 2.1-wide roof gets 7 tabs on even rows and 6 plus half-tabs on odd rows for coverage.

Still planning the color variation for tabs and now sketching a fascia board along the front edge of the roof.

I'm adding small cream bunting spheres along the fascia edge, then checking the roof corner geometry at each wall position to make sure the tabs line up correctly—I'm noticing the back corner calculation puts a point too close to the tower, inside rather than along the edge, so I need to fix that overlap.

Checking whether the roof geometry clears the sail lattice near the front face, and confirming the porch rails at the lower u-range don't intersect either — both come out with sufficient clearance.

Now adding a glowing round window above the door: a torus for the frame (since its default orientation already faces the wall normal, no rotation needed) and a short cylinder rotated to serve as the glass pane.

I'm also adding cross muntins from thin dark wood boxes, a cream sill below the window, and calculating the nameplate position on the wall relative to the door's arch geometry.

Checking the gap between the keystone top and nameplate, I'm sizing the plate with engraved ink marks and small gold bolts at the ends, aligning it against the window frame ring below.

Working through the keystone geometry now, I'm positioning it to span the radial gap just outside the door's inner edge so the frame blocks sit flush without overlapping the recessed door slab.

For the arch voussoirs, I'm laying out nine blocks every 20 degrees from 10° to 170°, with the 90° block serving as the keystone, and sizing each block's tangential width so they slightly overlap at the inner radius while staying flush at the outer edge—since they share the same color, the small overlaps won't be visible.

Alternating colors would expose z-fighting since the overlapping blocks sit at the same depth, so I'm offsetting even and odd blocks' depth slightly (0.2 vs 0.21) to avoid coplanar flickering, though I'm also considering skipping alternation entirely and relying on the keystone and seam lines instead. For the frame, I'm embedding it 0.05 into the wall with a depth of 0.2, and now setting up the jambs running from the floor up to near the top of the opening.

Now I'm working out the door's positioning—jamb coordinates relative to the wall's slant, threshold height tying into the floor slab, and how the frame's bottom edge lines up with the floor at v=0.1 so it sits flush against the slab top.

Adding a slight bevel to the arch, then working out plank line spacing across the door and positioning the round window above it so it clears the arch top with margin to spare.

I'm adjusting the plank lines so they avoid clashing with the window ring, shortening them beneath the window and extending others up to meet the curved arch top with a small gap. Then I'm sketching in the door's hardware, placing diagonal strap hinges running from the hinge-side edge toward the center.

Adding hinge barrels, gold rivets, and a knob with rosette and escutcheon detail near the door, then starting on the window ring geometry.

I should also add a plaster patch on the tower wall section, and figure out placement for two sacks beside the porch steps, working out their world coordinates so they stay within the corner boundary constraints.

Checking sack placements: one at w=3.2,u=-1.2 works with w-u=4.4, and a second at u=-1.55,w=2.85 lands beside the stoop but outside the plinth's apothem radius, so it's clear. Moving on to position the barrel near u=+1.3.

Testing a barrel at u=1.3, w=2.85 with radius 0.27 — checking its diagonal extents against the building bounds, x comes out to about 3.2 and z to about 1.37, which fits within the 3.2 x-limit.

I'm also confirming the barrel sits clear of the roof edge above the porch and clear of the octagonal plinth face at x=2.5, landing just outside it at roughly 2.66, so the placement works.

Now I'm designing the sacks: a squashed sphere body scaled vertically and flattened on one axis to sit flush on the floor, topped with a tapered cylindrical neck, a small wooden tie ring, a flared cone for the frilled opening, and a tiny ink-mark patch on the front to suggest a label.

Adding label details... Then I'm working out how to vary each sack's orientation by rotating it around the Y axis, and sketching a small helper closure to compose positions and rotations for each sack's local frame.

Defining frame objects...

Now I'm designing the sack frame with its own origin and yaw rotation, then sketching a Fr class with constructor and put/sub helper methods for placing geometry. For the barrel shape, I'm approximating the bulge by stacking frustums of varying radii rather than using a single straight cylinder.

Still adding barrel details...

Now designing the hanging lantern at the header: a chain running down to a ring, a conical metal roof cap, a glowing yellow glass box for the light, and thin metal corner posts with a bottom plate to frame it.

I'm also considering a small decorative touch - a terracotta pot with a pink flower placed on the step's edge for extra charm.

Checking triangle budget: the spheres and flowers add up to roughly 2400 extra tris, well within the 12000 limit. Skipping bunting and door numbers as unnecessary extras, and verifying the roof peak stays under the max height bound at 2.75.

Recalculating the roof slope so it clears the lamp post, header, and brackets properly: I adjust the surface start and tab offsets so the top lands right at 2.75, then work out header, post, bracket, and lantern positions so they stack correctly beneath the roof overhang, with the lantern settling around y=1.84.

Now checking the window ring against the wall surface—its top collides with the roof underside, so I lower the window center and shrink the ring to keep it clear. That pushes the nameplate placement into conflict with the window bottom, so I'm reconsidering the layout, maybe hanging the nameplate from the porch header beam like a shop sign instead of stacking it above the door.

Working through the vertical layout, I find there's actually room for a small nameplate between the keystone top and the window ring if I shrink the door to about 1.05m tall and 0.86m wide — a bit chunky but workable given the porch ceiling and roof constraints. I'm now second-guessing whether to drop the round window altogether to reduce crowding.

Working out the round window's ring and glass dimensions, plus a sill box beneath it and whether to skip smaller details like muntins or an eyebrow arc. I'm deciding to keep the nameplate on the header and considering giving the keystone a small gold accent stud for detail.

Now I'm setting up the build with Three.js imports, pulling in geometry merging utilities and a glow helper, and planning to follow the template's Ctx typing conventions for the joint and property data even without explicit imports.

Still building geometry helpers...

Finishing the put function, it applies the combined rotation and position transform, either rendering as a standalone part with the "flat" option or baking the matrix directly into the geometry. I'm checking that the bone type should reference an actual joint like doorHinge rather than a generic mill placeholder.

I'm defining helper functions for box, cylinder, sphere, torus, and cone geometries to simplify part creation, and noting that merging geometries requires consistent index attributes across them.

Now I'm setting up coordinate frames for the base and wall (the wall tilted by a lean angle), then starting to build the footing and floor sections, placing stone blocks and adding seam/course details like dark mortar lines and alternating vertical joints on the footing's front face.

Placing more seam lines...

Now checking the door mat dimensions and positioning the cream border bars and center stripe relative to the doorway at w=2.2, with the mat itself spanning w 2.55 to 2.9 so it doesn't overlap the door.

I'm also placing a potted flower bush on the second step with a layered pot, dark rim, soil, and three small flower tops in pink and gold for color variety. Next I'll move on to building out the posts, header, brackets, rails, and flower boxes, then the roof structure.

Writing roof geometry helper...

Checking the offset math for row i=5 and i=0 confirms the tab heights line up correctly with the roof surface at those widths, and the front row's tab just barely stays within the edge boundary. Now I'm working out the along-row tab spacing, alternating positions for even rows across seven tabs.

Still writing roof tiling logic...

Now placing the side bargeboards along the roof slope, positioning them so they align just under the tab tops with a slight upward offset. I'm also considering adding underside rafters beneath the dark teal roof slab so the structure reads correctly from low viewing angles.

Checking the height alignment where the roof base meets the header—confirming the header top touches the roof bottom at 2.18. I'm now adding the door header itself along with a nameplate panel and border trim mounted on its front face.

Still adding details... small ink marks for lettering, gold bolt accents at the ends, then moving on to the door frame jambs with cream trim positioned around the wall opening, accounting for where the arch begins.

Now I'm working out the arch segments: a series of radial blocks placed at increasing angles around the arch, alternating cream trim and plaster coloring, with a slightly larger keystone block at the center top.

Checking the jamb inner boundary against the arc's inner radius confirms they align, though the block width creates a slight angular overlap with neighboring wedges at the inner face—this should stay hidden since adjacent blocks occupy that same space.

Still defining door geometry...

Adding more plank geometry...

Working out the round window placement, making sure the glass sits inside the ring hole and figuring the vertical center using the wall's slope math. Adding a sill below the window and considering whether to skip extra decorative details like keystones or flower accents to keep things simple.

Now adding small gold rivets around the ring and a stud at the keystone, deciding to skip extra dot trim along the arch. Moving on to set up the lantern's sub-frame using a rotated transform off the main frame.

Working out the lantern chain, ring, and cap positions...

Adding the glass box with glow, corner posts, base plate, and inner flame sphere, then checking the overall lantern sits correctly above head clearance before computing its x-position from the frame offset.

Now I'm building the sacks using PF.sub, sizing the body sphere with a slight scale for a flattened shape, adjusting the center so the bottom actually touches the ground, then adding a neck cylinder and a tie torus for the drawstring.

Adding frill and label details...

The slight gap in the label's position against the sack surface seems acceptable, so I'll settle on a fixed height with a small tilt. For the second sack, I'm planning to generalize the geometry into a reusable function that takes a scale factor so the dimensions and positions scale proportionally for a smaller version.

Now I'm checking placement coordinates to keep the second sack within the box bounds, but each adjustment either pushes the x-position too low or the z-extent too far past the 3.2 limit, so I need to find a position that satisfies both constraints simultaneously.

Checking the second sack position against the plinth boundary and sail arm clearance—it seems to clear both, though it's slightly outside the preferred box. I'm now considering an alternative: stacking the two sacks against each other instead, adjusting their coordinates to see if that fits more cleanly.

Checking the sack placement against the door jamb and mat boundaries, I find shifting it to w=2.7 avoids the frame overlap while staying clear of the mat zone, so I'll settle sack2 on the porch slab there, clear of the rail balusters.

Sack1 goes near the ground steps at (-1.2, 3.0) for variety. For the barrel, I'm positioning it at u=1.3, w=2.85 with enough radius clearance from the porch edge, and building a local subframe for its details — adding a small lid cylinder on top in a light wood tone, though I'll skip extra decorative elements like a scoop or sprig to keep it simple.

Actually, I decide to make the barrel more charming: instead of a plain lid, I'll use a rim torus for the barrel edge plus a dark wood disc inset, filled with three or four red apple spheres arranged in a circle with one centered, making it look like an open barrel of apples. I'm also planning the metal hoop rings around the barrel body using thin torus shapes rotated to wrap horizontally, matching the radius profile of the barrel's frustum shape at different heights.

I'm calculating the exact radius of the barrel at each hoop height so the torus rings sit flush against the tapered wood, slightly oversized so they visually sit outside the barrel's faceted surface rather than clipping into it.

Now I'm designing a flower box function: a wooden crate shape with a slightly lighter rim and a darker soil layer inset near the top, positioned centered along the rail, with plans to loop through placing flower stems spaced evenly inside.

I'm tallying up the total color count across the palette to stay under the 64-color limit, deciding to reuse existing colors like woodDark for soil rather than adding custom ones. I'm also considering small charm details like a leafy vine climbing the porch post with alternating leaf spheres and pink flowers, keeping additions modest.

Checking for z-fighting and verifying the door frame embeds properly into the tower wall geometry without conflicting with the plaster patch. I'm also confirming the glow import path and making sure the solo part return type handles the null case correctly when wrapping it in glow().

Now I'm writing a helper that generates an arch outline as a sequence of points, tracing the base corners up and around a semicircular arc, making sure the winding order stays counter-clockwise for the extrude function to work correctly.

Placing post pieces...

Now working out the bracket orientation: I need the angled brace to point from each post toward the center, so I'm setting the rotation sign based on which side (s=+1 or s=-1) the post is on, verifying the geometry math confirms the angle direction is correct for both sides.

I'm adding a spiral of small leaf shapes climbing one of the posts, then placing two horizontal rail bars across the gate at different heights.

Adding balusters...

Checking that the rails align properly with the posts and door jambs, verifying the top rail height for the flower box origin, and noting the lantern bracket is already handled before assembling the final code.

Now adding details for the wall ring window, door rivets with gold spheres, and strap hinge barrels, while deciding on plank line and kick band colors before finalizing the doorstep threshold slab.

I'm merging all the collected geometry buckets into parts with their assigned colors and bones, then moving on to building the roof tabs loop that computes tab widths and offsets for each of six segments...

Writing roof tab geometry...

Still working out roof geometry...

For the bunting I'm placing eleven small scaled spheres along the fascia bottom edge to create scallop decorations, aligning them to the fascia's y-position. Then I'm cross-checking the wall frame origin against the door center coordinates to confirm they align, and confirming the door's window ring sits flat in the door plane with no extra rotation while cylinders get a 90-degree rotation to lie flat as disks.

Now I'm moving into final code assembly, keeping the `P` type loose for flexibility.

spec.name: Dutch Windmill (Animal Crossing)
spec.description: A chunky, pastel, storybook Dutch tower windmill with a gallery deck, a teal shingled cap, four striped cloth sails and a tail pole, built in an Animal Crossing toy-diorama style.
spec.layout:
STYLE: Animal Crossing. Everything is chunky, rounded and toy-like: thick trim, oversized round-topped windows and door, soft pastel flat colours, warm woods, no thin or fussy parts. Edges get fat lighter 'highlight' strips or darker 'outline' strips as small parts. Repeating motif: a small TULIP (three-petal red or yellow head on a green stem, with two leaves) plus a LEAF. It appears on the door, the sail cloth, the signboard, the cap boards and the planters.

COORDINATES: +Y up, front +Z, left +X, centred on x=0. All values are metres. The tower is an OCTAGONAL tapering prism with a FLAT FACE toward +Z, so faces point at yaw 0, 45, 90... degrees. Apothem = distance centre to flat face. Circumradius = apothem / 0.924. For a lathe with 8 segments, spin it 22.5 degrees so a flat face looks to +Z.

STACK FROM THE GROUND UP:
1) Stone plinth: octagon, apothem 3.3, y 0 to 1.0 (tower part).
2) Walls: apothem 3.0 at y=1.0 tapering linearly to 2.15 at y=8.6. Apothem(y) = 3.0 - 0.1118*(y-1). Cream plaster with a brick-red band at y 4.6-4.9 and a brick-red cornice at y 7.9-8.6 (tower part).
3) Gallery deck: octagon, apothem 3.7, slab y 2.2 to 2.5, railing at apothem 3.55 reaching y 3.5, corbel brackets under it, stairs up the +X side (gallery part).
4) Cap: round, rim radius 2.7 at y 8.6, onion-dome of teal shingles rising to a peak at y 11.6, gold finial and weathervane to y 12.5 (cap part). A nose housing covers the windshaft at the front, to z 3.2.
5) Windshaft and sails: horizontal axle along +Z at y=9.6 from z 2.6 to the hub at z 4.0. Four sails in an X pose at 45, 135, 225 and 315 degrees from up. Each stock is 6.2 m long from the hub. The sail plane is z 4.0 to 4.3 and a spinner cone ends at z 4.9. The lowest sail tip is at y of about 4.6, well above the gallery railing, and the sails clear the tower.
6) Tail pole (staart): a ladder-like beam from the cap back at [0,9.0,-2.55] sloping down to the ground at [0,0.35,-6.6], with a capstan winch beside its foot (tail part).
7) Door yard: the arched door with its porch frame on the front face under the gallery deck, plus planters, barrels, sacks, a hanging lantern and a signboard (doorYard part).

FRONT TO BACK: sail plane z 4.0-4.3 and spinner to z 4.9, door yard z 2.9-4.6, gallery and tower (centred at z 0), cap, tail pole going back and down to z -7.0. Resting on the floor: plinth, stair bottoms, door yard props, tail pole foot and capstan.

SILHOUETTE: a squat, wide plump tower, a big round teal hat, huge cheerful sails with cream cloth and coral stripes. Windows are warm-glowing. The model reads like a cozy village landmark.

parts.builds: The octagonal body (flat face to +Z, dimensions as in layout). Stone plinth (plinthStone, y 0-1.0, apothem 3.3) with a plinthDark chamfer course on top and a few lighter stones as small parts. Tapering wallCream walls (apothem 3.0 at y 1.0 to 2.15 at y 8.6) built as a loft or a stack of frusta. Brick-red band (brick, with brickDark course lines and small brick blocks) at y 4.6-4.9. A brick cornice (brick, brickDark underside) at y 7.9-8.6. Fat trimWhite corner pilasters on all 8 edges, slightly proud of the walls. Soft wallShade horizontal plaster lines every ~0.9 m. The door porch on the front face: a trimWhite surround box x -0.85..0.85, y 0-2.15, z 2.9-3.5, with a doorTeal arched plank door in it (vertical plank lines in woodDark, a gold knob, a tulip emblem above the door in tulipRed with leaf leaves, a round little transom window). All of this stays below the gallery deck at y 2.2. Chunky round-topped windows (glass panes lit with glowWarm inside, trimWhite frame, doorTeal shutters on both sides, woodLight sill with a tiny tulip pot) at yaw 0 and +-45 degrees at y 5.7, at yaw +-90 degrees at y 4.3 and at yaw +-135 degrees at y 6.9. Also small round glass port-holes at y 7.3 on yaw 0 and 180. A back round window at yaw 180 at y 5.7. The walls at the top end in a trimWhite ring where the cap sits at y 8.6.
parts.attaches: Rides joint base. Gallery deck sits on mount galleryDeck (y 2.4) around its walls; the cap rests on towerTop/capRing; the door porch is at doorCenter.

parts.builds: The wraparound gallery (stage) at mount galleryDeck. Octagonal deck slab (woodWarm top, woodDark edge fascia, apothem 3.7, y 2.2-2.5) with plank seam lines as thin woodDark strips. Under it, 8 chunky angled corbel brackets (woodLight) going from the wall to the deck underside, one per face, plus a woodDark rim board. Railing at apothem 3.55: woodLight posts at every corner and midpoint, with a top rail (woodLight) at y 3.5 and a mid rail at y 3.0 (trimWhite). Leave a gap in the railing where the stairs land at the +X side. A turned finial ball on each corner post. Stairs on the +X side, x 3.6-5.0 and z -1.8 to 3.6, going up from the ground at mount galleryStairBottom (z 3.6, y 0) to the deck at galleryStairTop (z -1.2, y 2.4): 8 treads (woodWarm, rise 0.3, run 0.6) on two woodDark stringers, a landing platform at deck level, a handrail (woodLight) with posts along the outer side, and a hanging tulip-motif board (tulipRed tulip on a trimWhite plank) at the landing. Small iron lantern hooks at the deck underside, and two coils of rope hung on the railing in woodLight.
parts.attaches: Rides joint base. Deck centres on galleryDeck and wraps the tower walls (do not rebuild walls). The door porch sits beneath it, and door-yard props stay below y 2.2 in front. The deck leaves room for the cap above.

parts.builds: The turning cap (rides joint cap). A trimWhite and woodDark rim ring at y 8.6-8.9, radius 2.7. Above it, a round onion dome (lathe, 16 segments, radius 2.6 at the rim, up to a peak at y 11.6) clad in roofTeal shingles. Stack 6 rows of scalloped shingle bands (alternating roofTeal and roofTealDark) as flattened rings or half-discs seated on the dome. A gold ring at the peak with a gold acorn finial to y 12.2 and a weathervane to y 12.5: an iron rod, a gold arrow and a tiny tulipRed tulip cut-out. Two round gabled dormer windows at yaw +-70 degrees from front (glass glowing glowWarm, trimWhite frames, roofTealDark mini hoods), and one small hatch at the back. The front nose housing (woodWarm box, woodLight rounded front with a trimWhite collar, z 2.0-3.2, around the shaft at mount shaftBase y 9.6) blends into the dome. At the back, a woodDark beam stub and an iron bracket mark the tailRoot mount [0,9.0,-2.55]. Three small tulipRed/tulipYellow tulip emblems on trimWhite boards around the rim.
parts.attaches: Rides joint cap. Sits on the tower top at capRing/towerTop. The windshaft (sails part) enters the nose housing at shaftBase. The tail pole attaches at tailRoot.

parts.builds: The windshaft and four sails (rides joint sailHub, pivot at mount hub [0,9.6,4.0]). A woodDark axle along +Z from z 2.6 to the hub. A gold bearing collar at z 3.3. The hub: a chunky woodWarm cylinder disc, radius 0.5, z 3.85-4.35, with a trimWhite rim and 8 iron bolt dots. A rounded spinner nose cone in tulipRed, z 4.3-4.9, with a gold tip ball. Four identical sails at 45, 135, 225 and 315 degrees from up (X pose), each built the same way: a main stock beam of woodWarm (square 0.2 section, 6.2 m long from the hub centre, centred at z 4.1) with a woodLight highlight stripe on it. spec.name: Dutch Windmill (Animal Crossing)
spec.description: A chubby, cozy Animal Crossing style Dutch windmill with a stone base, tapered thatched-brick tower, rotating cap and four lattice sails, on its own small footprint.
spec.layout: Squat, rounded octagonal tower tapering upward, centred on x=0, facing +Z. A wide stone plinth sits on the floor, then a cream plastered brick body with a red-brown trim band, a front door with a little step, round-top windows and a balcony (gallery) ring partway up. A domed red-roofed cap sits on top with a small tail pole and ladder at the back, and a hub on the front (+Z) of the cap carries four big wooden lattice sails in an X shape, tilted slightly toward the viewer. Everything is chunky and soft with bevelled, faceted primitives; flat pastel colours, warm tops and cooler undersides, little props like flower boxes, a lantern and a sack of flour at the door.

parts.builds: Stone plinth (octagonal, two stacked tiers in stone/stoneDark with stone block seams as small parts), small grass tuft ring hugging the plinth, flagstone path stub to the door, and the door step. Keep simple, sized to the footprint.
parts.attaches: Top at plinthTop; tower stands on towerBase; path ends at doorFront.

parts.builds: Tapered octagonal tower from radius ~1.55 at the base to ~1.05 at the top in wall cream, with a brick-coloured lower skirt band, trimWood bands at bottom, mid and top, vertical corner ribs in wallShade, small brick patches, and a rounded top ring. Includes the gallery balcony ring at galleryDeck (wood deck, posts, rail).
parts.attaches: Stands on towerBase; cap sits on towerTop; door and windows are mounted on its surface by the detail part.

parts.builds: Front door in teal with a round top, frame, planks, golden knob and hinges, a lantern beside it glowing, a sack of flour and barrel by the door. Round-top windows (windowFrame surround, window glass, shutters in teal, cross bars) at three heights around the tower, flower boxes with pink and yellow flowers and leaves under the front windows, and a small loft hatch.
parts.attaches: Seated on the tower surface at doorFront and around the tower; rides base joint.

parts.builds: Domed cap on capCentre: a roof lathe in roof red with lighter shingle rows as small parts, a trim ring at the eaves, a tiny finial with a golden ball on top, a small round gable window, the front axle housing and hub boss at hubFront, and at the back a tail pole with a ladder (wood rails and rungs) running down toward the ground.
parts.attaches: Sits on towerTop; hub at hubFront connects to the sails joint; tail pole ends at tailPoleBack.

parts.builds: Four big lattice sails of sailFrame wood crossing at a spinning hub at hubFront: each has a long main spar, a thinner outer rail, many cross-bars and cream sailCloth panels on the leading half in alternating neat patches, a rounded tip cap, and small colour pennant ribbons on the tips (roof and flowerYellow). A hub cap in darkWood with golden nail studs. Arms extend ~2.2 m from the hub, tilted slightly outward, one pair vertical and one horizontal in rest pose (plus-shape rotated 45 degrees to an X), all rigid on the sails joint.
parts.attaches: Centred on mount hubFront, riding the sails joint.
